answer.evidence: Each wall and tower has a flagstone walk or platform about 10-11 rows deep, with a crenellated back parapet (light rows 17-19, 49-51). The platform ends in a dark front-edge line (row 27 on the tower, row 59 on the wall). Eave shadow rows sit below that line, then the ashlar front face (rows 60-79 on the north wall, longer on the towers and gatehouses) with arrow slits, doors and arches. The west and east walls are seen from above as flagstone tops. The gatehouses have crenellated top platforms. The brazier, crates, stone balls and pennant are decor on the platforms. The silhouette widens and steps in a consistent 3/4 profile.

styleAnswer.evidence: The candidate has 12 visible tones per tile, matching house-h101_0 (12) and above house-h112_0-stone (10). Near-flat coverage is 2%, close to the references' 0%. Only 10% of its dark edge pixels are near-neutral, similar to the references' 7-9%, so the outlines are dark brown-tan tints of the sandstone rather than a black sticker line. By eye, the ashlar blocks are shaded one by one with highlight, mid and shadow edges, plus speckled grain on the orange-brown parapet and wall-walk areas. The cobbled road, the crenellations, the wooden doors, the iron portcullis and the stair shadows all carry varied tones. The sandstone ramp is slightly narrower than the roof-tile ramps in the references, at about 5 steps against 6, but it is not shallow. Large flat areas are absent, so the piece would sit acceptably next to the references.

answer.evidence: The wall ring and towers each have a crenellated flagstone top band. At x=208 and x=303 the top runs rows 48/51-58 and ends in a dark front-edge line at row 59. Eave shadow and a tall ashlar front face follow, about 84 rows on the north wall (rows 60-143) and rows 224-319 on the south wall. Gatehouse and tower platforms each show a top surface above a front face. The stairs, arch tunnel and door are all drawn as front faces under those tops. The side walls are seen from above, with no receding isometric side face. Trapdoor, brazier, crates, balls and pennant are decor.

styleAnswer.evidence: The sandstone ramp has about 5 steps: pale highlight cap on the merlons and block tops, light tan, mid tan, orange-ochre weathered patches, and a dark brown shadow. The shadow runs down the inner wall faces and under the towers. Each ashlar block is shaded individually with its own top highlight and lower edge, and the wall-walk tops carry speckle grain. The outlines and joints are tinted dark brown-tan, not neutral; only 10% of dark edge pixels are near-neutral, against 7% and 9% for the references. Measured density matches the references: 12 visible tones per tile against 12 and 10, with 2% near-flat coverage against 0%. No large flat fills show; the walls, arch, doors, stairs and gravel road all carry variation. The wall ring is a larger structure than the houses, but it is the same building kind and is drawn at the same pixel scale. A careful artist would accept it beside the references. It is slightly more uniform in block pattern than the roof tiles of the references, but not shallower.

answer.evidence: The north and south walls show a walkway band with a crenellated parapet (rows ~49-58). It ends in a dark edge line (column x=208 row 59, #4e3d30) followed by dark eave shadow, with a 4-tile weathered ashlar face below (rows ~60-80 on the north wall). The towers and both gatehouses have platforms with a flagstone floor and a front-edge line (e.g. x=112 row 27 #4e3d30, x=208 row 59, x=303 row 59). Below each platform is a tall front face with arrow slits, a barred window and doors or arch. The west and east walls are seen from above as flagstone tops. This is a 3/4 view with real top surfaces and front faces.

styleAnswer.evidence: The candidate's visible tones per 16x16 tile (12) match house-h101_0 (12) and exceed house-h112_0-stone (10). Near-flat coverage is 2%, close to the references' 0%, so there are no real flat fills. Only 10% of dark edge pixels are neutral, in line with the references' 7-9%. The outlines lean brown and are dark sandstone tones, not a black sticker line. The ashlar blocks have several sandstone steps (highlight, light, mid, shadow, deep), with speckled grain on the orange upper wall-walk and per-block edge highlights. Cobbled road dots and cast-shadow bands add variety. The candidate is still a little less rich than the references. Its raw palette is only 56 colours against 185 and 66. The stone faces are somewhat regular and repetitive, and the large wall faces rely on block-line patterns more than varied grain. The references have more per-tile tile-by-tile highlights and speckle. Overall it is a close match to the Beodeul craft, but marginally lighter in detail.

A flagstone walkway (rows 60-78, orange tone) follows, then a dark front-edge line at row 79. Below it is a weathered ashlar front face with a shadow base, rows 80-143, which is far more than 3 rows. The towers have crenellated top platforms with an edge line and arrow-slit faces below. The west and east walls show their tops from above. The decor on the platforms is listed as decor. styleAnswer.evidence: The candidate's sandstone ramps show about 5 steps: a pale highlight on the merlons and block tops, light and mid sandstone, a dark shadow side, and a deep shadow in the arch and stair. Edges are tinted brown-tan beside the stone, and the measured near-neutral dark-edge share is 10%, similar to the references' 7-9%, so this is not a sticker outline. Visible tones per tile are 12, equal to h101 and above h112 (10). Near-flat coverage is 2%, close to the references' 0%. Texture comes from the ashlar block joints, per-block speckle, the grainy orange-tan wall-walk flagstones, and the cobble road. Some large wall faces are fairly uniform blocks with light grain, and there is less per-tile highlighting and clumping than the references' roof tiles, so it reads a little less rich overall. It is still within the quality bar and would sit acceptably next to the references.
